content.introduction: The sources indicate that Outlook-at-Risk quantifies risks around future real GDP growth, unemployment rate, and inflation based on financial conditions. For real GDP growth and CPI inflation, it considers risks around the average quarterly growth rate over the next four quarters, while for the unemployment rate, it considers risks around the quarterly average in four quarters’ time. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) has increased the target range for the federal funds rate by 4.50 percentage points since March 2022. The unemployment rate was at 4.2% in August, slightly above June projections. The sources do not provide a definitive answer regarding specific future projections beyond the noted figures and trends.
body: Outlook-at-Risk provides an objective way of quantifying the risks around future real GDP growth, the unemployment rate, and inflation by capturing how such risks evolve as financial conditions ease or tighten. [...] For real GDP growth and CPI inflation, Outlook-at-Risk considers risks around the average quarterly growth rate over the next four quarters; however, for the unemployment rate it considers risks around the quarterly average in four quarters’ time. Why the difference? The time series of real GDP growth and CPI inflation are subject to considerable quarter-to-quarter transitory variability that can be “smoothed out” by taking averages over multiple quarters. In contrast, the unemployment rate has [...] In the spirit of this work, Outlook-at-Risk follows a similar methodological approach and estimates the conditional distribution of future real gross domestic product (GDP) growth, the unemployment rate, and consumer price index (CPI) inflation based on contemporaneous financial conditions for each month since January 1989.

Since the last projections were released, economic growth has been above expectations, the unemployment rate is slightly above expectations, and inflation lower than expected (although there are some "base effects" that might push PCE inflation up a little later this year).

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) has increased the target range for the federal funds rate by 4.50 percentage points since March 16, 2022. In tightening the stance of monetary policy, the FOMC balances the risk of inflation remaining persistently high if the economy continues to run “hot” against the risk of unemployment rising as the economy cools.
